segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that their hearts may be encouraged, as they are knit together in love and come to all the riches of the full assurance that understanding brings, to the knowledge of God’s secret, Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this so that no one may mislead you with plausible arguments.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I am absent in the flesh, I am still with you in spirit, rejoicing as I see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, just as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: rooted and being built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, overflowing with thanksgiving.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not done by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when you were dead in your offenses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our offenses,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wiping out the record of debt that stood against us with its regulations and was opposed to us; he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stripped the rulers and the authorities and exposed them publicly, leading them in triumph by the cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let anyone judge you over food or drink, or in the matter of a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one who delights in self-abasement and the worship of angels disqualify you—someone who goes into detail about what he has seen, puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and does not hold fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that comes from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to regulations:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: about things that are all destined to perish with use—according to human commands and teachings?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Such things have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-chosen worship, self-abasement, and harsh treatment of the body, but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

notes.note: Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established technical term. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose, and Paul stresses that it has now been made known. “Mystery” today suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, so “secret” is used; the lexicons give it as a primary gloss.

notes.traditional: the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ
notes.note: The manuscripts give this phrase in more than a dozen forms, including “of God”, “of God, which is Christ” and the longer wording behind the King James Version. The short and abrupt “of God, of Christ”, found in the earliest witnesses, is generally judged original because it best explains why scribes produced the others. Most interpreters take “Christ” as identifying the secret, as the translation does, though the grammar would also allow “the secret of the God of Christ”.

The meaning of this phrase is disputed. In Greek of the period it normally meant the physical elements of which the world is made (earth, water, air, fire); the word could also mean elementary principles, the ABCs of a subject. Many modern versions render “elemental spirits” or “elemental spiritual forces”, taking the elements as personal powers, but clear evidence for that use is later than Paul. The translation keeps the plain term and leaves the question open.

The phrase can mean the circumcision that Christ performs or that belongs to him, a spiritual counterpart to the physical rite. It can also mean the circumcision Christ himself underwent, that is, his death, pictured as the stripping off of his body of flesh, in which believers share. The translation leaves both possibilities open.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person, and its meaning is not disputed. “Trespass”, the usual rendering, now chiefly suggests entering property without permission, so “offense” is used; the King James Version itself has “offence” for this word in Romans 5.

The Greek word was the everyday term for a handwritten note acknowledging a debt, signed by the debtor. Ink could be washed or wiped off papyrus, which gives “wiping out” its force. Interpreters differ on whether the “regulations” attached to it are the commandments of the Law of Moses or a more general statement of obligations.

The verb belongs to the same word family as “stripping off” in verse 11. Most modern versions take it to mean that God stripped the powers of their weapons or dignity, hence “disarmed”; the King James Version has “spoiled”. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take the form to mean “stripped off from himself”, as one throws off a garment. “Stripped” keeps the link with verse 11 and fits the image of captives displayed in a victory parade.

notes.phrase: leading them in triumph by the cross
notes.note: The verb refers to the Roman triumph, the procession in which a victorious general paraded his defeated enemies through the city as a public spectacle. The Greek ends with a pronoun that can mean “in it”, the cross just mentioned, or “in him”, Christ. The translation takes it as the cross and names it for clarity; a good number of versions and scholars prefer “in him”.

The Greek word is “body”, the same word used throughout this chapter. Shadow and body was a common way of contrasting an outline or foreshadowing with the solid reality that casts it, and “substance” gives that sense. Paul may also intend an echo of the body of Christ, which he mentions in verse 19.

The word ordinarily means humility and is a virtue in 3:12. Here and in verse 23 it names something the rival teachers pride themselves on and is linked with harsh treatment of the body, so most scholars think it refers to practices of self-denial such as fasting, for which “humbling oneself” was a regular expression in Jewish Greek. Versions vary among “humility”, “false humility”, “asceticism” and “self-abasement”.

The traditional reading is worship offered to angels. The Greek can equally mean the worship that angels themselves offer, which visionaries claimed to witness or join; Jewish visionary writings of the period show great interest in the heavenly liturgy. Scholars are divided, and the English phrase is left as open as the Greek.

notes.phrase: goes into detail about what he has seen
notes.traditional: intruding into those things which he hath not seen
notes.note: This clause is among the most obscure in the letter. The verb can mean to enter, to set foot on, or to investigate in detail, and it is also found in inscriptions for entering a sanctuary after initiation; so the sense may be “which he saw on entering”, referring to visionary experiences. The King James Version follows later manuscripts that add “not” (“things which he hath not seen”); the earliest manuscripts lack it.

notes.phrase: but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh
notes.traditional: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh
notes.note: The Greek of this verse is compressed and its syntax is disputed. The rendering given follows the majority of modern versions: the rules look wise but do nothing to check self-indulgence. Others take it to mean that the rules are of no value and serve only to gratify the flesh, that is, they feed human pride. Either way Paul’s verdict on the regulations is negative.

candidates.reason: The phrase τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου recurs in Galatians 4:3, 9 and versions split between “elements”, “elementary principles” and “elemental spirits”, with related uses in Hebrews 5:12 and 2 Peter 3:10, 12.

It occurs across the whole New Testament in senses from the physical body to human nature opposed to God, and versions vary widely (“flesh”, “body”, “sinful nature”, “human”); readers need a consistent policy.
The figurative sense of conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and translators divide between keeping the Semitic idiom “walk” and rendering “live”.
It is a virtue (“humility”) in most occurrences but a criticized practice in Colossians 2:18, 23, so the register should fix when each rendering applies.

In the recurring pair ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι (Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 15, Ephesians, Colossians) versions vary among “rulers”, “principalities”, “powers” and “rule”, and the pair should be rendered uniformly.
